evidence_quotes.quote: Newtok is one of many villages across rural Alaska that does not have an in-home piped treated water and sewer system.

For this analysis, I focus on the patterns that emerge around household domestic water access, preferred sources for drinking, the subjective lived experiences of water insecurity including risk perceptions, and the daily work and social relationships involved in accessing water and hygiene practices.

Although not explored in depth in this article, such dynamics would include the local arrangements of social power involved in water access, as well as the larger political economic processes determining infrastructure funding and subjectivities involved in treated water access (for example, see Eichelberger 2011, 2014).

Over the course of 6 days in July 2016, I conducted participant observation and semi-structured, open-ended interviews in person with 16 residents, including 11 heads of household and several tribal leaders (broadly defined as both tribal council members and individuals employed by the Newtok Village Council) in Newtok, Alaska.

According the water plant data, Newtok’s average per capita treated water consumption is 1.91 gal/c/day. This rate is far below the WHO minimum standard for water security of 13.2 gal/c/day (Howard and Bartram 2003).

criterion_notes.c1: Yes. Examines household domestic water access and sanitation conditions in Newtok, Alaska, an unplumbed rural Alaska Native village where households self-haul water from the community water treatment plant, school, rainwater, and distant natural water sources, and use honey buckets for human waste.
criterion_notes.c2: No under both readings. Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study does not investigate a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor as an exposure: the author explicitly states that political-economic and institutional power dynamics around infrastructure funding and relocation are 'not explored in depth in this article' and 'described elsewhere' (p. 4), focusing instead on cultural meanings, traditional ecological knowledge, risk perceptions, gender/age roles, and interpersonal kinship/reciprocity relations (Table 2, p. 8). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading, no eligibility rule, administrative burden, documentation/tenure requirement, tariff/cost-recovery rule (water at the plant is hauled 'for no charge', p. 5), enforcement practice, or regulatory structure directly governing service access is analysed; brief descriptive mentions of unused state-installed tanks settling into unstable ground (p. 6), employee-only school showers in houses excluded from the study (p. 6), and a 10-gallon-per-household daily conservation cap at the school during a 5-day power outage (p. 7) are incidental context rather than an analysed rule-type mechanism.
criterion_notes.c3: Yes. Primary empirical ethnographic study conducted in July 2016 combining participant observation, semi-structured interviews (23 individuals: 16 Newtok residents representing 10 self-hauling households and 7 external informants), coded with MAXQDA, alongside monthly water treatment plant consumption records.
criterion_notes.c4: Yes. Reports quantitative community-wide treated water consumption (1.91 gal/c/day from plant records; 1.82 gal/c/day theoretical maximum during emergency school rationing) as well as qualitative outcomes on seasonal household water availability, reliance on untreated sources, and household water rationing/reuse.
criterion_notes.c5: Yes. Population and unit of analysis (households and individuals in Newtok, Alaska; 10 self-hauling households / 16 resident interviewees plus community-level utility data), exposures (cultural dimensions, risk perceptions, seasonal/physical storage constraints, and interpersonal kinship/sharing networks), outcomes (domestic water access, per-capita treated water consumption, and water conservation/source-selection practices), and study design (exploratory ethnographic qualitative/mixed-methods case study) are clearly identifiable, though the exposure falls outside Criterion 2.

study_design: Exploratory ethnographic field study (participant observation, semi-structured interviews using convenience sampling, and community water plant consumption records)
population_and_sample: Yupik community of Newtok, Alaska (~350-384 residents, 66 households); convenience sample of 23 interviewees comprising 16 Newtok residents across 10 self-hauling households (including 11 heads of household and tribal leaders) and 7 external informants involved in relocation, water system, or public health
exposure: Cultural dimensions of water insecurity, traditional ecological knowledge, risk perceptions of treated versus natural water, physical/seasonal water plant storage limits, vehicle access, gender/age roles, and interpersonal kinship/reciprocity hydro-social networks
outcome: Household domestic water access, community-wide per capita treated water consumption (1.91 gal/c/day; 1.82 gal/c/day theoretical cap during plant shutdowns), seasonal reliance on rainwater/natural sources, and household water rationing/reuse practices
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). While this empirical ethnographic study examines household water access and consumption outcomes in an unplumbed Alaska Native community (satisfying c1, c3, c4, c5, and c6), its analysed exposures are cultural meanings, traditional ecological knowledge, risk perceptions, gender/age hauling roles, physical/seasonal storage limits, and interpersonal kinship/reciprocity networks. Political, institutional, and regulatory governance factors are explicitly set aside as outside the scope of the article (p. 4), failing Criterion 2 under both its plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism scope.
